newsitem.title: INDIA: Non-aligned seek to end U.N. Security Council veto.
newsitem.headline: Non-aligned seek to end U.N. Security Council veto.

text.p: Foreign Ministers of the 113-nation Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) on Tuesday demanded action to eliminate the U.N. Security Council veto, describing it as discriminatory.

"The use of the veto should be curtailed with a view to its eventual elimination," the ministers said in a declaration on reforms in the United Nations adopted in New Delhi on the last day of their two-day meeting.
"There shall be no partial or selective expansion or enlargement of the Security Council to the detriment of the developing countries," the declaration said.

There is a currently a proposal pending in a U.N. working group to expand the Security Council, whose five permanent members have the veto power to shoot down proposals without a majority in the council.
The five are the United States, Britain, China, France and Russia.

Leading members of the movement of developing countries say that the veto power is often used to defeat proposals from other nations in the U.N. General Assembly, in which all U.N. members have equal representation.

Foreign Secretary Salman Haider, the most senior Indian diplomatic official, told a news conference that there was "not anything beyond normal" in differences between NAM members before the unanimous adoption of the declaration.

He said there was no move to spell out aspects of curtailment of the current veto powers, since the declaration was a statement of intention. "This declaration is addressed to an essential principle," he said.

The statement on the veto was a key part of the NAM's call for democratic reforms in the United Nations that received backing on Monday from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who attended the inauguration of the ministerial conference.
South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo told a news conference on Tuesday that the veto power was discriminatory.
"It is grossly undemocratic that the fortunes of millions of people of the world are given to a few people to decide," Nzo said.
In a caustic attack on Monday, Zimbabwe Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge said his country opposed efforts to enlarge the Security Council with new permanent members who would not enjoy veto powers.
"In the bovine kingdom a castrated male is not called a bull but a steer....A permanent member without a veto power, is, in Security Council terms, a steer and not a bull," he said.

"We should not accept a permanent member category made up of bulls, comprising the victorious allies from World War II, and the steers, made up of those chosen as a result of the current reform of the U.N. Either they are all bulls or they are all steers," he said.
Mudenge also cautioned against some NAM members lobbying "for permanent seats we have not yet won".
"This runs the risk of putting our common objective completely out of reach and threatens to scatter our common quest," he said.
India is among countries seeking a permanent seat on the council. Indian officials said they had no comment on the Zimbabwean position.
